findings.where: The blue 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' band straight after the hero: its white 'Subscribe' button
findings.fault: The Subscribe button is a link to #subscribe, and the page has no sign-up form and no email field to land on. A visitor who presses it jumps to the band they are already in, and nothing happens. The page offers an action it cannot do.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer who wants Mark's briefings presses Subscribe, gets no form and no confirmation, and is left unsure whether they signed up. A dead control on an advisor's own site also makes the site look unfinished.

findings.where: First screen and the band directly below it: the 'Write to me directly' address block against the full-width blue Subscribe field
findings.fault: The brief asks for one action. The first scroll shows two, and the second carries more weight: a whole field of house blue with a large white serif heading and a white button, against the smaller blue box holding the address. Squint at the first screen and the scroll after it, and the strongest action is Subscribe, not writing to Mark. The visual order does not match the task order.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose brief allows one direct, personal way to reach Mark. A visitor deciding whether to contact Mark is pulled toward a newsletter sign-up instead.

findings.where: Header on the first screen (desktop and phone): 'Mark M. Moseley' and the MMM Infra mark
findings.fault: The header has no navigation at all, only the name and the logo, and the logo just returns to the top. The palette says mist is used for 'nav links', but none are drawn. From the first screen a visitor has no route to his articles, PDFs, background or contact.
findings.who_objects: A visitor checking Mark's standing looks to the top of the page for his writing and talks and finds nothing to follow. The founder asked for nav as part of the hero, exactly as a visitor sees it.

findings.where: Article specimen: the 'Streamlining the PPP Process' lecture card with its download arrow and 'PDF' label
findings.fault: The card promises a download (an arrow icon and 'PDF'), but the whole card is a link to #article on the same page. Pressing it downloads nothing and opens no document, so the download look sits on an in-page jump.
findings.who_objects: A reader who wants the lecture presses PDF and gets no file. The research calls the PDF list 'the product', so a card whose signifier lies about what it does undermines the very depth the page is meant to show.

findings.where: Article specimen: the blue list numbers 1–3; style tile: the blue tracked 'PALETTE' label
findings.fault: The page states 'blue only where something can be clicked', yet it uses the link blue on parts nobody can act on: the list numbers and the PALETTE eyebrow. The colour reserved for links is borrowed by static text, so blue stops meaning one thing.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of Mark's articles may try a blue number or label and find it does nothing. Angélique, following the stated rule as she adds content, gets a rule the tile itself breaks.

findings.fault: This is a button that replays the animation where you are, but it wears the link look (blue, underlined) that the footer's email link also wears. One treatment means both 'go somewhere' and 'do something here'.
findings.who_objects: Few visitors would notice. Anyone reviewing the tile who expects a link to navigate would be briefly surprised when nothing leaves the page.
